en: The Sūtra on the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, at Mount Kuṇḍala, amidst the Fearful Forest.

In a place where deer gathered among the trees, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—five hundred bhikṣus who were all noble sages having attained supernatural powers, all venerable bhikṣus, whose names were as follows:

The Venerable Aññātakondañña, the Venerable Assaji, the Venerable Vappa, the Venerable Mahānāma, the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Bhagu, the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Uruvelakassapa, the Venerable Nadīkassapa, the Venerable Gayākassapa, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Moggallāna, the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable Rāhula—such as these were the five hundred bhikkhus.
Furthermore, there were five hundred bodhisattvas, such as Maitreya and others, whose names were:

Bodhisattva Increaser of Resolve, Bodhisattva Firm Resolve, Bodhisattva Accumulation of Eloquence, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Śrīprabha, Bodhisattva Mṛduśrī, Bodhisattva Ṛddhipuṣpa, Bodhisattva Śūnyatābhūta, Bodhisattva Prāmodyaśuddha, Bodhisattva Indrabhūmi, Bodhisattva Yaśobhūmi, Bodhisattva Mṛdusvaranirghoṣa, Bodhisattva Śuddhabhūmi, Bodhisattva Parvatacaya, Bodhisattva Sampanna, and Bodhisattva Indraśrī. Such were the five hundred bodhisattvas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; O God among Gods, if you would grant me leave to do so, I shall venture to inquire."
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“I shall grant you leave to ask; inquire whatever you desire, and the Tathāgata will respond according to your wishes, causing your heart to rejoice.”
Thereupon, having been granted permission to ask his question, Maitreya Bodhisattva leaped for joy and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How many dharmas must a bodhisattva practice so that they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates?"
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Maitreya!
It is because the Bodhisattva has great compassion and seeks the well-being of many, taking pity on all devas and humans, that he has resolved to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning as this.
"Listen attentively!
Constantly keep this in mind!
Maitreya then spoke:
“Yes, World-Honored One; we shall receive your instruction and listen.
The Buddha said: “Maitreya!
Bodhisattvas possess one practice that abandons all evil realms and prevents them from following after evil associates.
What is this one?
It is the mind of the path of tranquil equanimity.
"This is the first dharma.
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Furthermore, there are two practices that abandon the evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are these two?
First, abiding in meditative concentration without any arising;
second, employing skillful means to distinguish all that is seen.
"These are the two dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas of practice for a bodhisattva, by which they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are the three?
First, attaining the dharma of great compassion;
second, practicing nothing within emptiness.
"Third, there is no conceptualization regarding that which is known.
These are the three dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
“Furthermore, there are four practices of a bodhisattva by which they abandon the evil realms and do not follow after evil associates.
What are these four?
First, establishing oneself in the precepts;”
Second, having no doubts regarding any phenomena;
third, delighting in dwelling in seclusion;
fourth, practicing equanimous contemplation.
"These are the four dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are five practices for a bodhisattva by which they abandon the evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are the five?
First, constantly establishing virtue and righteousness;
second, not seeking out the shortcomings of others.
Third, to examine one's own conduct;
fourth, to always delight in the Dharma;
fifth, not to be preoccupied with one's own body but to constantly rescue others.
"These are the five dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas of practice for a bodhisattva, by which one abandons all evil realms and does not follow after evil associates."
What are the six?
First, being free from stinginess and greed;
second, eliminating the mind of wickedness.
Third, they are free from delusion;
fourth, they are free from coarse speech;
fifth, their minds are like space.
"Sixth, taking emptiness as one's abode.
These are the six dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
“Furthermore, there are seven practices of a bodhisattva by which they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates.
What are these seven?
First, possessing a mind of skillful means;”
Second, being able to discern the various jewels of the Dharma;
third, constant diligence;
fourth, constant joy.
Fifth, attaining patient acceptance through faith;
sixth, skillfully understanding the concentrated mind;
seventh, possessing the total illumination of wisdom.
"These are the seven dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are eight dharmas of practice for a bodhisattva, by which they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are the eight?
First, attaining right view;
second, right mindfulness;
Third, right speech;
fourth, right action;
fifth, right livelihood;
Sixth, right effort;
seventh, right intention;
eighth, right concentration.
"These are the eight dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are nine dharmas of practice for a bodhisattva, by which they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are the nine?

First, the bodhisattva, being liberated from desire and having distanced himself from all evil and unwholesome dharmas, is free from conceptualization; attaining the joy of tranquil concentration, he practices the first *ekāgratā* (one-pointedness of mind).

Second, having eliminated conceptualization, his internal mind becomes tranquil and his mind becomes one; being without thought and without activity, he attains a concentrated state of mind and experiences mental rapture, practicing the second *ekāgratā*.

Third, being free from joy and contemplating with constant tranquility, the body attains serenity like that of the noble ones; what is spoken and contemplated does not give rise to mental activity, and one practices the third *ekāgratā*.

Fourth, having already severed suffering and pleasure, both elation and dejection have completely ceased; what is contemplated is neither painful nor pleasant, and the mind is pure, as one attains the fourth *ekāgratā*.
Fifth, one transcends perceptions of form;
Sixth, there is no longer any conceptualization;
seventh, one no longer dwells on various perceptions, fully entering the wisdom of infinite space;
eighth, having transcended the wisdom of infinite space, one enters the practice of the cognition and awareness of immeasurable consciousnesses.

Ninth, they transcend all wisdoms that know through consciousness, and no longer harbor notions of existence or non-existence; they transcend all wisdoms that lack consciousness, thereby entering the practice of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and not perceiving perception as they attain the samādhi of tranquility.
"These are the nine dharmas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"Furthermore, there are ten dharma-practices for a bodhisattva, by which they abandon all evil realms and do not follow after evil associates."
What are the ten?
First, attaining the vajra-samādhi;
second, the samādhi of progress and benefit in whatever place one dwells;
Third, attaining the samādhi of skillful means and instruction;
fourth, attaining the samādhi of governing and delivering through mindfulness and non-mindfulness;
fifth, attaining the samādhi of pervading the world.
Sixth, they attain the samādhi of equanimity toward suffering and pleasure;
seventh, they attain the Jewel Moon Samādhi;
eighth, they attain the Moonlight Samādhi.
Ninth, they attain the Illumination Samādhi;
tenth, they attain the Twofold Tranquility Samādhi, being fully endowed with all dharmas.
Maitreya!
"These are the ten dharma-practices of a bodhisattva, by which one abandons all evil realms and does not fall among evil associates.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One, in his former lives, practiced generosity, Giving away his wife and children, as well as food and drink."
Not begrudging head or eyes, the Buddha’s virtue is the Perfection of Liberation;
Guarding the prohibitions without transgression, like the peacock cherishing its plumage,
his observance of the precepts is peerless— this is the Perfection of Merit.
Having already manifested the power of patience, he regards all suffering and pleasure as equal;
with forbearance as his great strength, the Buddha’s virtue is the *pāramitā* of patience.
Having fully realized the power of diligence, his unsurpassed virtue confronts all harm.
Vigor is the great arrival; the Buddha’s diligence is the *apramāṇa* of crossing over.
Having severed all evils, the Guide delights in one-pointedness of mind;
with great wisdom and tranquility as his power, the Buddha’s purity is the *apramāṇa* of crossing over.
Pure wisdom is sovereign, spontaneously arising from nowhere;
wisdom is eternally supreme—this is the Buddha’s Perfection of Wisdom.
With wisdom he subdues the hosts of Māra; beneath the tree, he attains great insight.
The supreme meaning is free from all defilements; by the Buddha’s power, Māra is subdued.
The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma and lets out the great lion’s roar;
he terrifies and subdues all non-Buddhists, for the Buddha’s wisdom delivers them to virtue.
His physical form is wondrous and peerless; his virtue of precepts and his wisdom are likewise.
Having crossed to the further shore through diligence, the Buddha-way surpasses all other virtues;
it is difficult to illustrate and beyond metaphor. This is the unsurpassed, great wisdom.
"Constantly expounding the treasures of all dharmas, with radiant light he guides and leads the multitudes.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!"

This is because Maitreya Bodhisattva’s vows are fully realized; his preaching of the Dharma is without deficiency, and he expounds the words and phrases of the Dharma with equanimity. The phrases of the Dharma he teaches are free from all attachment and bondage, and when he finishes preaching the sutra, there is no confusion.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Ānanda!”
"As it has been said, Maitreya Bodhisattva is fully endowed with eloquence, and the sūtras and dharmas he expounds are without deficiency.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"

Maitreya Bodhisattva did not merely praise me with these verses; rather, in the past, ten incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Jvalanaprabhāsa-rāja-saṃgha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently present as one who has accomplished wisdom and conduct, Stable One, Father of the World, Unsurpassed Being, Charioteer of the Dharma, Honored One above gods and men, Buddha, God among Gods. At that time, there was a son of a brahmin elder named Bhadracaryā, who, coming out from a park, saw from afar the Tathāgata walking in meditation, his body radiant with light in countless transformations.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"How excellent!
This is truly unprecedented!"

The body of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; it is so majestic, with its wondrous and excellent radiance and divine splendor, adorned with the virtue of auspiciousness. I vow that in a future life, may my own body likewise be fully endowed with such radiance and divine splendor, and adorned by the virtue of auspiciousness.
Having made this vow, he prostrated himself on the ground and thought with deep sincerity:
"If, in a future age, I shall attain the Dharma-body as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, may the Tathāgata pass over my body."

At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King Endowed with Radiant Light, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the brahmin youth, the son of a householder named Virtuous Conduct, passed over his body.
After he had traveled to Yue, he immediately attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereupon, the Buddha turned back and addressed his attendant, saying:

"The reason I passed over the body of the brahmin youth Bhadrapāla was to cause him to immediately attain the patience of non-arising, so that his eyes could see through all things, his ears could hear with penetrating clarity, he could know the thoughts within the minds of others, he could know from where he himself had come to be born, and his body could fly, being fully endowed with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)."

As soon as the Buddha passed over the body of the brahmin Bhadravarga, he immediately attained all-knowledge and was fully endowed with the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) without any loss. He then praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
"Coming and going through the worlds of the ten directions, The Honored One among men has no equal.
Your mind is set only on the Way, transcending all conditioned phenomena; I pray that you, the Awakened Guide, receive my prostration."
Surpassing the luminosity of all worlds, And the blazing radiance of mani-jewels, The Buddha’s light is supreme; I prostrate to the Awakened Guide.
Just as when a lion lets out a single roar, all small beasts submit without exception;
so too does the Buddha preach the Dharma, completely subduing all those of other paths.
The mark between his eyebrows is pure and penetrating; his majestic presence is immeasurable, like accumulated snow.
His radiance illuminates the three realms; while the Buddha dwells in the world, none can equal him.
Beneath the feet of the Sage are born the marks of the wheel; these wheels are wondrous, possessing a thousand spokes.
Neither this land nor its hills and mounds can move the Unsurpassed Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who the son of a householder, the brahmin and virtuous practitioner, was at that time, it is none other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya."
The venerable Ānanda then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Bodhisattva Maitreya has attained the patience of non-arising for such a long time; why does he not swiftly reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“There are four matters for which a bodhisattva does not attain perfect awakening.
What are these four?
First, purifying the buddha-field;
second, protecting the buddha-field;
third, purifying all things.
The fourth is to protect all beings.
These are the four matters.
When Maitreya Bodhisattva sought Buddhahood, he did not accept it because of these four matters.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
When I was originally seeking Buddhahood, I also desired to purify the buddha-field and to purify all beings; I also desired to protect the buddha-field and to protect all beings.”

Maitreya conceived the aspiration for enlightenment forty-two kalpas prior to me; I conceived the aspiration for the Way only after him. Through great diligence during this Bhadrakalpa, I have transcended nine kalpas to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told the venerable Ānanda:
"I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment through ten matters.
What are these ten?"
First, all that one possesses without any sense of attachment;
second, one's wife;
third, one's children.
Fourth, head and eyes;
fifth, hands and feet;
sixth, kingdom and territory.
Seventh, precious jewels and wealth;
eighth, marrow and brain;
ninth, blood and flesh.
Tenth, not begrudging one's own body or life.
Ānanda! By means of these ten matters, I quickly attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Furthermore, there are ten things by which one quickly attains the Way of the Buddha. What are these ten?
First, to establish oneself in virtuous conduct through the Dharma;
second, to constantly practice patience;
third, to constantly practice diligence.
Fourth, always keeping the mind unified;
fifth, constantly practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
sixth, never abandoning anything.
Seventh, having attained the mind of patience, one regards all things with equanimity;
eighth, one does not practice emptiness [as a conceptual object];
ninth, one attains the patient acceptance of the dharma of emptiness.
Tenth, one attains the dharma of non-conceptualization.
Ānanda! By means of these ten matters, I have personally attained the Way of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the worthy Ānanda:
"When I originally sought the path to Buddhahood, I underwent countless hardships and austerities before attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way; these matters were not few."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"In a past age, there was a prince named Sarvārthadarśin (All-Meaning-Manifest), who was handsome and of exquisite beauty. As he was leaving a park and garden, he saw on the road a man afflicted with a grave and critical illness. Upon seeing him, he felt a heart of sorrow and compassion, and asked the sick man:
'By what medicine can you be treated so as to recover immediately?'"
The sick man replied,
"Only the blood from Your Majesty's own body can cure my illness.
Thereupon, the Prince immediately pierced his body with a sharp blade to draw out blood and gave it to the patient, bestowing it with a sincere heart and without any regret.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"At that time, Prince Xiànyì was none other than my own self. Ānanda!"
"The waters of the four great oceans may still be measured by the bushel, but the blood I have given as an offering cannot be reckoned.
Why is this? It is because I seek perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha spoke thus to the worthy Ānanda:

"In a past age, there was a prince named King Padma. He was handsome and fair, with a majestic and towering presence. While traveling out from his park for an excursion, he saw on the road a man whose body was afflicted with leprosy. Upon seeing him, he immediately felt a heart of compassion and asked the sick man:
'What medicine can cure your illness?'"
The sick man replied, "If I could obtain the marrow from the King's body to anoint my own, my illness would be cured.
At that time, the Prince immediately broke his own bones to obtain the marrow and gave it to the sick man; he bestowed the gift with joy, his heart free of regret.
"At that time, the crown prince was none other than my own self.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The waters of the four great oceans may still be measured in bushels, but the marrow of my body given as alms cannot be reckoned."
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

"In a past age, there was a king named Candraprabha (Moonlight), who was handsome and fair, with majestic and towering divine power. As he was leaving his palace, he saw along the road a blind man, impoverished and starving, begging for alms. The man approached the king and addressed him, saying:
'Your Majesty alone is honored, noble, secure, and happy; I alone am impoverished and, moreover, blind.'"
At that time, King Candraprabha saw this blind man and, moved by compassion, tears fell from his eyes as he said to the blind man:
"What medicine is there that can cure your illness?"
The blind man replied, "Only by obtaining the King's eyes can my illness be cured; only then shall my eyes see.
At that time, King Candraprabha took out his own two eyes and bestowed them upon the blind man, his mind remaining tranquil without a single thought of regret.
"The King Candraprabha was none other than my own self.
The Buddha said,
"Mount Sumeru may still be weighed to know its exact mass, but the gift of my eyes cannot be measured or calculated."
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

"When Maitreya Bodhisattva originally sought the Way, he did not attain the path to Buddhahood by giving away his ears, nose, head, eyes, hands, feet, body, life, precious treasures, cities, wives, children, or kingdoms as alms to others. Rather, he attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path through the practice of peaceful bliss and skillful means."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“By what skillful means does the Bodhisattva Maitreya attain the path of Buddhahood?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“Maitreya Bodhisattva, three times each day and night, properly adjusted his robes and bound his body, joined his palms with his knees touching the ground, and addressed the ten directions with these verses:
‘I repent of all my transgressions, and I encourage and assist the virtues of the multitude.
I take refuge in and pay homage to all Buddhas, so that they may attain unsurpassed wisdom.’”
The Buddha said to the worthy Ānanda:
"By means of such skillful means, Maitreya Bodhisattva has attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme perfect enlightenment."
"Ānanda! This was the fundamental vow made by Maitreya Bodhisattva when seeking the Way:

'When I become a Buddha, may the people in my land be free from all defilements and impurities; may they not be greatly burdened by lust, anger, and ignorance, and may they diligently practice the ten wholesome deeds. Only then shall I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.'"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In future ages, the people will be free from defilement and will practice the ten wholesome deeds; they will not allow lust, anger, or delusion to occupy their minds."
At that very moment, Maitreya shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and realize supreme perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? It is due to the power of the original vows of the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

“When I was originally seeking the bodhisattva path, I desired to protect all beings so that they might all attain purity; yet they dwelt amidst the five turbidities of lust, anger, and delusion, taking pleasure in birth and death.”

Why is this? Because these people for the most part act contrary to the Dharma, taking what is wrong to be right; they follow deviant paths and harm one another, being unfilial toward their parents and constantly harboring evil thoughts. They harbor malicious intentions toward their brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, and others; they treat their teachers and preceptors with contempt, constantly committing impure acts against men, and devouring one another. [The Bodhisattva] vows to appear as a Buddha during such a time and age.

In the commanderies, kingdoms, villages, and towns, people speak only of various evils and how they harm one another; they strike each other with tiles and stones, lash each other with staves, and gather together to revile one another. Returning to their own homes, they prepare food and drink, placing poison within it with the intent to harm others. Their thoughts become defiled and turbid as they give rise to slander; they conceal their faults and evils only to reveal them to one another, until no further good intentions remain.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Out of great compassion, I universally keep all beings in mind and preach the Dharma for the sake of such people as these.
When the worthy Ānanda heard the Buddha say this, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly unprecedented!

O God among Gods, Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you are able to exert diligent effort and universally expand your great resolve to discipline the wicked and bring them to accomplishment; having removed their heavy burdens and endowed them with the treasure of the Dharma, you preach this sutra and its teachings for the sake of such people."
The Buddha said, "So it is, Ānanda!
It is as you have said; the Buddha can endure this."

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, in order to transform those who are stubborn and fierce and to eliminate their manifold darkness, and by virtue of being fully endowed with the merit of the Buddha-dharma, preached this sutra and its teaching for the sake of such a person.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Hearing that the Tathāgata’s firm and heavy diligence and equanimity are such as this, my hair stands on end.
What is the name of this sutra?”
"How should one practice and uphold it?
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "This sutra is named 'The Original Vow'; you should uphold it."
"You should properly uphold the *Maitreya-pūrvayoga-maitreya-paripṛcchā*.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and other great disciples, as well as the assembly of bodhisattvas and all those present—including devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and human beings—heard the sutra with joy and came forward to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva
